clue.text: GCSE hell may be produced by poet/ translator (of Shakespeare)

indicators.note: the letters of the exam phrase can be made to yield the name, so the phrase signals a rearrangement

parts.note: the eight letters of GCSE and hell are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dreadful time at school exams is blamed on a German poet who translated Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be produced by' signals the anagram of GCSE HELL. GCSEs are the exams English pupils sit at sixteen. August Wilhelm Schlegel translated much of Shakespeare into German.
explanation.definitionFit: August Wilhelm Schlegel was a German Romantic poet whose verse renderings of Shakespeare became the standard German texts.

clue.text: He drew attention to time spent under ground by under-age child

definitions.text: He drew attention to time spent under ground by under-age child

parts.words: He drew attention to time spent under ground by under-age child
parts.note: the author whose first draft was called Alice's Adventures Under Ground, about a young girl's stay below the earth, with a rabbit forever checking his watch

explanation.surface: Someone publicised how long a young child was kept below ground, like a rescue story.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis Carroll's manuscript gift to Alice Liddell was titled 'Alice's Adventures Under Ground'; the child is Alice, and time is drawn into it by the White Rabbit and the Mad Hatter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll wrote the underground adventures of the young Alice, and also illustrated that first manuscript himself.

clue.text: Aiken's view west of Bridges's paradise

definitions.text: Aiken's view west of Bridges's paradise

parts.words: Aiken's view west of Bridges's paradise
parts.note: the American poet Conrad Aiken wrote a poem whose title names a view lying west of Eden, the paradise

explanation.surface: A scenic outlook in the country, beyond a garden of bridges.
explanation.walkthrough: Conrad Aiken's long poem is 'Landscape West of Eden'; the clue paraphrases that title, with Eden glossed as the paradise of the poet Robert Bridges.
explanation.definitionFit: A view of countryside is a scene, the sense of the first word of Aiken's poem title.

clue.text: Greens may produce more than one style of art

definitions.text: more than one style of art

indicators.note: the word can be rearranged into another, so this phrase signals the letters being reworked

parts.note: taken as written, the six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Green paints may give rise to several distinct artistic styles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may produce' signals the anagram of GREENS.
explanation.definitionFit: Genres are categories or kinds, here styles of art in the plural.

clue.text: Colourful Chronicle of the Nineteenth Century

definitions.text: Colourful Chronicle of the Nineteenth Century

parts.words: Colourful Chronicle of the Nineteenth Century
parts.note: Stendhal's novel was subtitled 'Chronicle of the Nineteenth Century', and its title names two colours

explanation.surface: A vivid history of the 1800s.
explanation.walkthrough: Stendhal's 1830 novel 'The Red and the Black' bears the subtitle 'Chronique du XIXe siècle'; its title is red and black, hence colourful.
explanation.definitionFit: Stendhal's novel of Julien Sorel's ambitions carries that subtitle and is named after two colours, red and black.

clue.text: Pinter's ache not significant

definitions.meaning: Harold Pinter's one-act play is A ____ Ache

explanation.surface: A playwright's pain is nothing worth fussing over.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Pinter's radio play 'A Slight Ache' (1959) supplies the first definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something minor or trivial is of little importance, and Pinter's play title qualifies its ache with this word.

clue.text: German composer namely, with the name of Parry

parts.note: sc., short for Latin scilicet, means namely
the English composer Sir Hubert Parry, who set Jerusalem, had Hubert as his given name

explanation.surface: A German composer is identified by sharing a first name with Parry.
explanation.walkthrough: SC (scilicet, 'namely') goes before HUBERT, Parry's first name. Schubert was Austrian but German-speaking, hence the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Schubert, writer of the Unfinished Symphony, was a composer of the German-speaking tradition.

clue.text: Sort of stop to which Sam Weller may have come

definitions.text: Sort of stop to which Sam Weller may have come

parts.words: Sort of stop to which Sam Weller may have come
parts.note: Dickens's cockney servant in The Pickwick Papers would drop his consonants in the throat-closing way London speech does

explanation.surface: A kind of halt at which a Dickens character might have arrived, like a coach stop.
explanation.walkthrough: The glottal stop is the catch in the throat replacing a T in cockney speech ('bo'le' for bottle); Sam Weller is the cockney manservant in Dickens's 'The Pickwick Papers'.
explanation.definitionFit: A glottal stop is a consonant made by closing the vocal cords, typical of London working-class speech.

clue.text: Clemens's private eye?

parts.note: Samuel Clemens, writing as Mark Twain, had his boy hero turn sleuth in a sequel titled with the hero's name and the word Detective

explanation.surface: Which detective did a man named Clemens employ?
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Clemens wrote as Mark Twain; his 1896 story 'Tom Sawyer, Detective' made his boy hero a private eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Twain's boy hero turns investigator in the novella that adds the title Detective to his name.

clue.text: His work intended to produce a silk purse?

definitions.text: His work intended to produce a silk purse?

parts.words: His work intended to produce a silk purse?
parts.note: a silk purse is proverbially what you cannot make from a sow's ear

explanation.surface: A craftsman's labours were meant to turn out a fine silk purse.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says you can't make a silk purse out of a sow's ear; the clue casts the Scottish novelist A. J. Cronin's work as aimed at that.
explanation.definitionFit: A. J. Cronin was a Scottish doctor-turned-novelist whose books include The Citadel.

clue.text: He had rebellious subjects — destroyed a mob hero

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken apart, so these letters are wrecked and reassembled

parts.note: the eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A ruler facing revolt watched a mob destroy its hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroyed' signals the anagram of A MOB HERO. Rehoboam, son of Solomon, saw the ten northern tribes of Israel rebel against him (1 Kings 12).
explanation.definitionFit: Solomon's son, king of Judah, lost most of his kingdom when the northern tribes revolted.

clue.text: Judge of Jean-Jacques

parts.note: the philosopher's late dialogues are titled with his own surname as judge of his own first names

explanation.surface: A judge presiding over a man called Jean-Jacques.
explanation.walkthrough: Jean-Jacques Rousseau's late work 'Rousseau juge de Jean-Jacques' has him judging himself.
explanation.definitionFit: Rousseau wrote the self-examining dialogues in which he sits as judge of Jean-Jacques, that is, himself.

clue.text: One of Koch's big guns?

parts.note: the poet Kenneth Koch wrote a play named after a woman, the same name the German First World War howitzers bore

explanation.surface: One of the heavy artillery pieces belonging to a man named Koch.
explanation.walkthrough: Kenneth Koch's play 'Bertha' shares its name with 'Big Bertha', the giant German siege gun of 1914.
explanation.definitionFit: Big Bertha was the nickname of the huge Krupp howitzer, and Koch's play has the same name for its heroine.

clue.text: His anger was kindled against David he returns among bailed suspects

definitions.text: His anger was kindled against David

indicators.note: the letters go back the way they came, read right to left
the name lies within the following words' letters

explanation.surface: A man furious with David goes back to the suspects let out on bail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' puts the name inside 'bailed', and 'returns' reads it backwards: BAILE turned round. Eliab, David's eldest brother, was angry at him before Goliath (1 Samuel 17:28).
explanation.definitionFit: David's eldest brother scolded him for coming to watch the battle, the Bible saying his anger burned against the boy.

clue.text: Indiscriminately abuse born admirer of queen

indicators.note: used without discrimination, at random, so the letters are thrown together anyhow

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone born to abuse others without discrimination admires the queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indiscriminately' signals the anagram of ABUSE BORN. Enobarbus, in 'Antony and Cleopatra', gives the famous speech on Cleopatra in her barge.
explanation.definitionFit: Antony's friend in Shakespeare's play describes Cleopatra's beauty with open admiration.

clue.text: Leading illustrator, but said to be a wild one

definitions.text: Leading illustrator, but said to be a wild one

parts.words: Leading illustrator, but said to be a wild one
parts.note: the decadent artist of the 1890s who drew for The Yellow Book was reputed a scandalous, unruly figure

explanation.surface: A top illustrator who had a reputation for wildness.
explanation.walkthrough: Aubrey Beardsley, the leading black-and-white illustrator of the 1890s, was notorious for his erotic and grotesque drawings.
explanation.definitionFit: Aubrey Beardsley was the foremost illustrator of the Decadent movement, with a scandalous reputation.

clue.text: Life of Glasgow — well protected

definitions.meaning: the American novelist Ellen Glasgow wrote The ____ Life (1932)
kept safe from harm or hardship

explanation.surface: Life in a Scottish city is a well-protected one.
explanation.walkthrough: Glasgow is not the Scottish city but the Virginia novelist Ellen Glasgow, author of 'The Sheltered Life'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shielded from danger describes someone kept safe, and Ellen Glasgow's novel title uses the word for such a life.

clue.text: Ruler reveals Miss Dell with left winger

parts.note: Ethel M. Dell was a popular English romantic novelist
a red is a communist or socialist, someone on the left wing

explanation.surface: A ruler shows off a woman called Dell in the company of a left-wing politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Ethelred, King of England, is put together from ETHEL (the novelist Ethel M. Dell) and RED.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethelred the Unready was an Anglo-Saxon king of England.

clue.text: Face the East in entire Tao, perhaps

indicators.note: signals one possible arrangement of the letters rather than the words as written

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Turning eastward is the whole of Taoism, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals the anagram of ENTIRE TAO.
explanation.definitionFit: To orientate originally meant to turn towards the east, the rising sun.

clue.text: Told in poetry, the other way round

definitions.meaning: written as verse rather than prose, as two words

explanation.surface: A story recited as a poem is turned back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: Opposite or reversed is the mathematical sense, and split in two the word says recounted in lines of poetry.

clue.text: Fade out, like Marryat's uncomplicated seaman

definitions.meaning: to dwindle away, as in to ____ out
Captain Frederick Marryat's novel ... Simple follows a naive young midshipman; simple means uncomplicated

explanation.surface: An unsophisticated sailor from a Marryat novel simply fades away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'like' is a link word. Marryat's 1834 naval novel is 'Peter Simple', so the uncomplicated seaman is Peter.
explanation.definitionFit: To peter out means to dwindle, and Peter is the first name of Marryat's simple midshipman.

clue.text: "all the virtuous actions they express / Are but a new and worse / Of her some one thought…" (John Donne, Funeral Elegies)

definitions.text: "all the virtuous actions they express / Are but a new and worse / Of her some one thought…" (John Donne, Funeral Elegies)

parts.words: "all the virtuous actions they express / Are but a new and worse / Of her some one thought…" (John Donne, Funeral Elegies)
parts.note: a gap in Donne's lines is filled by the word for a fresh issue of a book, after 'new and worse'

explanation.surface: A quotation from Donne's Funeral Elegies with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word in Donne's 'A Funeral Elegy' is 'edition': virtuous deeds are a new and worse printing of one thought of hers.
explanation.definitionFit: A printing or version of a text is the publishing sense, used by Donne for a copy of her thought.

clue.text: Offered on some occasions by Nemerov

definitions.text: Offered on some occasions by Nemerov

parts.words: Offered on some occasions by Nemerov
parts.note: the American poet Howard Nemerov published a collection pairing short maxims with occasional verse

explanation.surface: Something presented now and then by a man called Nemerov.
explanation.walkthrough: Howard Nemerov's 1973 collection is 'Gnomes and Occasions'; a gnome here is a pithy maxim, not a garden figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnomes are aphorisms or short wise sayings, and Nemerov's book set them beside poems for occasions.

clue.text: Paternal variety acquired by Philip Stanhope and Laertes

definitions.text: Paternal variety acquired by Philip Stanhope and Laertes

parts.words: Paternal variety acquired by Philip Stanhope and Laertes
parts.note: Lord Chesterfield's letters to his son Philip Stanhope and Polonius's 'neither a borrower nor a lender be' to Laertes were fatherly counsel

explanation.surface: A kind of fatherly something passed on to two young men.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Chesterfield wrote his famous 'Letters to His Son', Philip Stanhope; in 'Hamlet', Polonius gives Laertes his precepts before he sails.
explanation.definitionFit: Counsel or guidance is what both fathers gave their sons, the paternal kind.

clue.text: "The world will have a generation of idiots", he said

definitions.text: "The world will have a generation of idiots", he said

parts.words: "The world will have a generation of idiots", he said
parts.note: a much-shared quotation, attributed to the physicist of relativity, fearing technology would overtake human interaction

explanation.surface: A gloomy prediction about a coming generation of fools.
explanation.walkthrough: The line, usually given as 'I fear the day that technology will surpass our human interaction', is popularly attributed to Albert Einstein.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Einstein, the physicist of relativity, is the man to whom the saying is popularly credited.

clue.text: He came most carefully upon his hour

definitions.text: He came most carefully upon his hour

parts.words: He came most carefully upon his hour
parts.note: in the opening lines of Hamlet the sentry Francisco tells his relief 'You come most carefully upon your hour'

explanation.surface: A punctual man arrived exactly on time.
explanation.walkthrough: At the start of 'Hamlet', Francisco greets the officer arriving for the midnight watch with 'You come most carefully upon your hour'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bernardo is the officer who relieves Francisco on the battlements of Elsinore in Hamlet's first scene.

clue.text: Nye's raptor magus?

parts.note: Robert Nye wrote a novel about Arthur's wizard, who shares his name with a small falcon

explanation.surface: Is a man called Nye's bird of prey also a wizard?
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Nye's 1978 novel 'Merlin' is about the Arthurian wizard, whose name is also that of a small falcon.
explanation.definitionFit: A merlin is a small falcon, and Merlin is Arthur's magician, the subject of Nye's novel.

clue.text: "So sweet love that April morn" (Bridges)

parts.note: a word is missing after 'love' in Robert Bridges's line, meaning appeared to be

explanation.surface: A line from a Bridges poem about love on an April morning.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Bridges's poem reads 'So sweet love seemed that April morn'; the solver supplies the missing verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means appeared, as love looked sweet that morning.

clue.text: Apparently in-house, depravity reported by Perry

definitions.text: Apparently in-house, depravity reported by Perry

parts.words: Apparently in-house, depravity reported by Perry
parts.note: a word for someone living in, followed by evil, depravity, makes a horror title

explanation.surface: Wickedness inside a household was apparently exposed by a man called Perry.
explanation.walkthrough: One living in the house is a resident; with evil (depravity) it gives 'Resident Evil', the title the clue points to.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident is a person who lives in a place, so in-house in the sense of living on the premises.
